title: Another kind of Lyapunov function for Volterra quadratic stochastic operators
statement: For the Volterra quadratic stochastic operator V(x)_k = x_k (1 + sum_i a_{ki} x_i) on the simplex S^{m-1}, with A = (a_{ki}) skew-symmetric and |a_{ki}| <= 1, does there exist another kind of Lyapunov function (beyond the known one) for V?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on Lyapunov functions for Volterra quadratic stochastic operators. The literature after 2009 (Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov, Rozikov and successors) continues to use the same logarithmic family and its variants; no fundamentally different Lyapunov function was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Derive the whole family of Lyapunov functions of logarithmic type directly, and see what the source's question is asking one to leave.
attempt.result: Take phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log x_i with c_i >= 0. Along the Volterra map, phi_c(V(x)) - phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log(1 + (Ax)_i), and since log(1+t) <= t this is at most <c, Ax> for every x in the simplex. So phi_c is nonincreasing along every trajectory as soon as <c, Ax> <= 0 for all x in the simplex, and in particular whenever A^T c = 0, in which case the bound is exactly 0 and phi_c decreases strictly unless (Ax)_i = 0 for every i with c_i > 0. This identifies the known Lyapunov family precisely as the nonnegative kernel of A^T, and shows the construction is exhausted by that kernel - which is why the source asks for another KIND. The concrete consequence: for a skew-symmetric A of full rank on the relevant subspace there is no such c at all, so those operators have no logarithmic Lyapunov function and are exactly where a new one is needed. A caution: this derivation is elementary and is presumably known to the authors; it is recorded because it delimits the search.
attempt.obstruction: Any Lyapunov function must be nonincreasing on all trajectories, and the Volterra dynamics preserves the faces of the simplex, so a candidate must degenerate on every face; the log family is the only elementary family with that property. Beyond it one is looking for a function whose increment is controlled by a quadratic rather than a linear form in x, and the sign of a general quadratic form on the simplex is not decidable from skew-symmetry alone.
attempt.key_identity: phi_c(V(x)) - phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log(1 + (Ax)_i) <= <c, Ax>, so sum_i c_i log x_i is a Lyapunov function exactly when c is a nonnegative vector with <c, Ax> <= 0 on the simplex, i.e. essentially when A^T c = 0.

title: Transversality for general quadratic stochastic operators
statement: A skew-symmetric matrix A is transversal if all its even-order leading principal minors are nonzero, and a Volterra QSO is transversal if its A is. Define a concept of transversality for an arbitrary QSO and find necessary and sufficient conditions on the matrix P = (P_{ij,k}) under which the QSO is transversal. (For Volterra QSOs, transversality implies that the fixed point set is finite.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on transversality for quadratic stochastic operators. No general definition beyond the Volterra case was found in the post-2009 literature. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what transversality is FOR, since the definition should be chosen so that the theorem it supports survives. In the Volterra case its consequence is finiteness of the fixed-point set.
attempt.result: Finiteness of the fixed point set is exactly transversality of the map x -> V(x) - x to zero, i.e. that 0 is a regular value of V - id on each face of the simplex. That is the definition that generalises, and it is intrinsic: it does not mention minors. For a Volterra QSO it specialises correctly because there V(x) - x = (x_i (Ax)_i)_i, whose zero set on the interior of a face is the solution set of a linear system with matrix a principal submatrix of A, and regularity of that system on all faces is precisely non-vanishing of the even-order principal minors (odd-order principal minors of a skew-symmetric matrix vanish automatically, which is why only even orders appear). So the source's minor condition is the Volterra shadow of 'zero is a regular value', and the general definition should be the latter. The remaining work - translating regularity into conditions on P - is a determinantal condition on the derivative DV(x) - I along the fixed-point set, which is not a condition on P alone.
attempt.obstruction: For a non-Volterra QSO the fixed-point equation is genuinely quadratic and its solution set is a variety rather than a linear subspace, so 'regular value' is a condition on P AND on the fixed point, not on P alone; a necessary and sufficient condition purely in terms of P would have to be an elimination-theoretic statement (a discriminant of the quadratic system), which exists in principle but is not a usable criterion for m >= 4.
attempt.key_identity: Odd-order principal minors of a skew-symmetric matrix vanish identically, which is why the Volterra transversality condition mentions only even orders; the intrinsic statement is that 0 is a regular value of V - id on every face.

title: Trajectories with periodic itinerary for Volterra quadratic stochastic operators
statement: For a transversal Volterra QSO the fixed point set X is finite, and it is known that a trajectory spends asymptotically all of its time in a neighbourhood U = U_1 union ... union U_t of the fixed points, visiting them in a sequence n_1, n_2, ... called the itinerary. Since X is finite the itinerary repeats values. Is there a trajectory with a PERIODIC itinerary?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on itineraries and heteroclinic cycles for Volterra quadratic stochastic operators and Lotka-Volterra maps. The heteroclinic-cycle literature for continuous-time Lotka-Volterra systems is extensive but I found no result on periodic itineraries for the discrete-time QSO. Kept open.

attempt.method: Recognise the object: a trajectory spending almost all its time near a finite set of saddles and moving between them is shadowing a heteroclinic network, and its itinerary is the sequence of nodes visited in that network.
attempt.result: A periodic itinerary is therefore a trajectory shadowing a heteroclinic CYCLE in the network whose nodes are the fixed points and whose edges are the connecting orbits. Two consequences follow immediately. First, existence requires the network to contain a cycle at all, which is a purely combinatorial condition on the signs of the eigenvalues of DV at each fixed point - checkable from A. Second, even when a cycle exists, the residence times near successive saddles grow geometrically with ratio the product of the ratios of contracting to expanding eigenvalues around the cycle, so the itinerary is periodic while the timing is not; the source's question is about the itinerary alone, which is exactly the shadowing statement and not an asymptotic-stability statement. Making that distinction is the useful step: one is asked for a periodic SYMBOL sequence, not a periodic orbit, and periodic orbits are typically absent while periodic itineraries need not be.
attempt.obstruction: Shadowing a heteroclinic cycle for infinite time requires the cycle to be asymptotically stable, and stability of a heteroclinic cycle depends on the ratio of eigenvalues around it exceeding one; for a skew-symmetric A those ratios are constrained but not obviously on the right side, and no criterion in terms of A is known. If the cycle is unstable, generic trajectories eventually leave and the itinerary is aperiodic.
attempt.key_identity: A periodic itinerary is a trajectory shadowing a heteroclinic cycle among the fixed points; its existence is governed by the product of contraction-to-expansion eigenvalue ratios around the cycle, not by the existence of a periodic orbit.

title: Sufficiency of the sign condition for Ulam's ergodic theorem for a three-dimensional Volterra operator
statement: For the Volterra QSO on S^2 given by x' = x(1 + ay - bz), y' = y(1 - ax + cz), z' = z(1 + bx - cy) with a,b,c in [-1,1], Theorem 3 states that if a, b, c all have the same sign and none is zero then Ulam's ergodic theorem (existence of the Cesaro limit of V^k(x)) FAILS. Is the negation of that condition sufficient for the ergodic theorem to hold?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on Ulam's ergodic conjecture for quadratic stochastic operators and the Zakharevich counterexample. Later work (Ganikhodzhaev-Zanin and successors) extends the failure to further parameter ranges; I found no proof that the complementary region satisfies the ergodic theorem. Kept open.

attempt.method: Identify the mechanism behind the failure in the known case and ask whether its negation is the right dividing line.
attempt.result: When a, b, c share a sign the three-species system is a cyclic (rock-paper-scissors) competition and the interior fixed point is a repeller, so trajectories spiral outward to the boundary heteroclinic cycle; the Cesaro averages then oscillate between the three vertices without converging, which is exactly Zakharevich's mechanism. If the signs are NOT all equal the cycle is broken - one of the three pairwise comparisons is reversed - so there is a transitive ordering on the three types and the dynamics is gradient-like, which is the situation in which Cesaro convergence should hold. So the source's dividing line is the presence or absence of a cyclic tournament, and the conjecture that its absence suffices is structurally plausible. What is missing, and it is not a technicality: the degenerate cases where one of a, b, c is zero leave a two-dimensional invariant face on which the argument must be run separately, and the source's condition excludes zeros only in the failure direction.
attempt.obstruction: Gradient-like behaviour gives convergence of trajectories to the fixed-point set but not convergence of Cesaro averages when the omega-limit set is a continuum, and a Volterra QSO with a degenerate a_{ij} can have a segment of fixed points. Ruling that out needs the transversality of Problem 2, which is itself unresolved for these operators.
attempt.key_identity: All three parameters of the same sign makes the tournament cyclic and the interior fixed point a repeller, which is Zakharevich's failure mechanism; mixed signs make the tournament transitive and the dynamics gradient-like.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for Ulam's ergodic theorem for general Volterra operators
statement: Find necessary and sufficient conditions on the skew-symmetric matrix A of a Volterra QSO under which the ergodic theorem (existence of lim (1/n) sum_{k<n} V^k(x)) holds on S^{m-1} for every initial point, for m >= 2.
status_search: Same search as E0061. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the tournament reading of E0061 and ask what the right generalisation of 'all signs equal' is for m > 3.
attempt.result: The sign pattern of a skew-symmetric A is a tournament on m vertices, and the Volterra dynamics on the simplex is the discrete-time analogue of the replicator dynamics for that tournament. For replicator dynamics the classical dichotomy is between tournaments that admit an interior evolutionarily stable point (the matrix game has an interior optimal strategy, equivalently the tournament has a Nash equilibrium with full support) and those that do not; the former have convergent time averages by the standard replicator time-average theorem, which says that if trajectories stay in a compact subset of the interior then the Cesaro limit is the interior equilibrium. So the natural conjecture, which the source does not state, is: the ergodic theorem holds for a Volterra QSO if and only if the associated tournament game has an interior optimal strategy, and it fails exactly when the game's optimal strategies live on a proper face. The m = 3 case of that conjecture is exactly Theorem 3 and Problem 4. This is a proposed criterion, not a theorem: the discrete-time replicator map does not obey the continuous-time time-average theorem, and that is where the work would be.
attempt.obstruction: The replicator time-average theorem is a continuous-time statement whose proof integrates d(log x_i)/dt; the discrete map replaces that derivative by log(1 + (Ax)_i), which differs from (Ax)_i at second order, and the accumulated second-order error over n steps is exactly of the same order as the quantity being averaged. Zakharevich's counterexample shows the error is not negligible.
attempt.key_identity: The sign pattern of the skew-symmetric A is a tournament and V is the discrete replicator map for it; in continuous time the Cesaro limit exists and equals the interior equilibrium whenever one exists, so the natural criterion is existence of an interior optimal strategy of the tournament game.

title: Do partition-type quadratic stochastic operators inherit the F-QSO fixed point theorem?
statement: For an F-QSO (E_0 = {0,1,...,m}, a set F of 'females' and its complement of 'males', with P_{ij,k} = 1 for k = 0 whenever i and j lie in the same class, and P_{ij,0} = alpha_0 for i in F, j in M) Theorem 5 states that the operator has the unique fixed point (1,0,...,0) and that every trajectory converges to it exponentially fast. Consider now a partition pi = {E_1,...,E_q} of E with P_{ij,k} = 0 whenever i and j lie in the same block; call this a pi-QSO. Is an analogue of Theorem 5 true for any pi-QSO?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on F-quadratic stochastic operators and partition (pi-) QSOs. Later papers on F-QSOs exist (Rozikov and coauthors) but I found none proving or refuting the pi-QSO analogue for general q. Kept open.

attempt.method: Test the q = 2 proof against q >= 3 by tracking why the 'empty body' state absorbs.
attempt.result: With two classes, any pair from the same class produces only the empty body 0, and reproduction requires one member of each class, so the mass at 0 is non-decreasing along the trajectory and strictly increases unless the population is concentrated in one class - which is why (1,0,...,0) is the unique fixed point and the convergence is exponential. With q >= 3 blocks the same monotonicity STILL holds, because P_{ij,k} = 0 for i and j in the same block forces those pairs to contribute to 0 as well, so x_0' >= sum_p (sum_{i in E_p} x_i)^2 >= 1/q by Cauchy-Schwarz. That gives an immediate quantitative statement the source does not record: for any pi-QSO the mass at the empty body satisfies x_0(n+1) >= 1/q, hence the trajectory enters and stays in the region {x_0 >= 1/q} after one step, and the convergence to (1,0,...,0) then follows from x_0' >= x_0^2 + 1/q(1-x_0)^2 whenever the cross terms cannot escape 0. This is a proof sketch of the analogue under the stated hypothesis and should be checked; the Cauchy-Schwarz step is exact but the last inequality assumes the cross-block coefficients sum to at most 1, which the definition permits but does not force.
attempt.obstruction: The definition of a pi-QSO constrains only same-block pairs; cross-block pairs may have arbitrary P_{ij,k}, so the mass produced at states other than 0 is uncontrolled and can be recycled into cross-block pairs at the next step. Whether that recycling can sustain a nontrivial fixed point is exactly what the Cauchy-Schwarz bound does not decide.
attempt.key_identity: For any partition into q blocks, Cauchy-Schwarz gives sum_p (sum_{i in E_p} x_i)^2 >= 1/q, so a pi-QSO puts mass at least 1/q on the empty body at every step - a uniform bound that does not depend on q's structure.

title: Fixed points and cycles of strictly non-Volterra operators in four or more types
statement: A strictly non-Volterra QSO satisfies P_{ij,k} = 0 whenever k is in {i,j}. For m = 3 every such operator has the form x' = alpha y^2 + c z^2 + 2yz, y' = a x^2 + d z^2 + 2xz, z' = b x^2 + beta y^2 + 2xy with a+b = c+d = alpha+beta = 1, and Theorem 6 states that (1) for all parameter values the operator has a unique fixed point, which is not attractive, and (2) the operator has 2-cycles and 3-cycles depending on the parameters. Is Theorem 6 true for m >= 4?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on strictly non-Volterra quadratic stochastic operators in dimension four and above. Papers on strictly non-Volterra QSOs on S^3 exist (Rozikov and coauthors, post-2009) and give partial classifications; I did not establish whether uniqueness and non-attractiveness of the fixed point are proved for all m >= 4. Kept admitted with that uncertainty recorded.

attempt.method: Ask which half of Theorem 6 is a counting statement and which is a stability statement, since they have different m-dependence.
attempt.result: Uniqueness of the fixed point is a Brouwer-plus-degree statement: V maps the simplex to itself continuously, so at least one fixed point exists for every m, and uniqueness is the assertion that the degree computation has no cancellation. Non-attractiveness is a spectral statement about DV at the fixed point, and here the strict non-Volterra structure gives something usable in every dimension: since P_{ij,k} = 0 for k in {i,j}, the diagonal of the derivative at any interior point vanishes in the sense that dV_k/dx_k = 2 sum_j P_{kj,k} x_j = 0, so DV has zero diagonal at every point of the simplex. A matrix with zero diagonal has trace zero, so the eigenvalues of DV at the fixed point sum to zero, and since DV also has row sums equal to 2 (Euler's relation for a homogeneous quadratic map restricted to the simplex), the spectrum cannot lie inside the unit disc unless the remaining eigenvalues are arranged to cancel a value of size 2 - which forces at least one eigenvalue of modulus at least 2/(m-1). For m = 3 that is 1, matching Theorem 6's non-attractiveness; for m >= 4 the bound 2/(m-1) drops below 1 and the argument no longer excludes attractiveness. That is a concrete reason to expect Theorem 6 to FAIL for large m, and it is not in the source.
attempt.obstruction: The bound 2/(m-1) is only a bound, so it does not construct an attracting example; producing one requires choosing P with all eigenvalues of DV inside the unit disc subject to zero diagonal and row sums 2, which is a feasibility problem that grows with m and has not been solved here.
attempt.key_identity: Strict non-Volterra means P_{ij,k} = 0 for k in {i,j}, so DV has zero diagonal everywhere; with row sums 2 this forces an eigenvalue of modulus at least 2/(m-1), which exceeds 1 only when m <= 3.

title: Exact regularity thresholds for quadratic stochastic operators
statement: For a QSO V with matrix P = (P_{ij,k}) on S^{m-1}, let lambda_m be the smallest number such that P_{ij,k} > lambda_m for all i,j,k implies V is regular (every trajectory converges to a unique fixed point). Theorem 7 gives lambda_m <= 1/(2m) and lambda_2 = (3 - sqrt(7))/2. Find the exact value of lambda_m for every m >= 3.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on regularity thresholds for quadratic stochastic operators. No exact value beyond m = 2 was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Check the two given data points against each other, since they are stated for the same quantity and should be consistent.
attempt.result: They are consistent but only just, and the comparison is informative. At m = 2 the general bound gives lambda_2 <= 1/4 = 0.25, while the exact value is (3 - sqrt(7))/2 = 0.17712..., so the general bound overshoots by about 41 per cent at the only point where both are known. Since the constraint sum_k P_{ij,k} = 1 forces P_{ij,k} <= 1 - (m-1) lambda for the threshold to be attainable at all, the admissible range of lambda_m shrinks like 1/m, and the exact value should behave like c/m for some constant c strictly below 1/2. The m = 2 datum suggests c is near 2 lambda_2 = 3 - sqrt(7) = 0.354, i.e. lambda_m of order 0.354/m rather than 0.5/m. That is a prediction with one data point behind it and should be treated as such - it is an extrapolation, not a derivation.
attempt.obstruction: The exact m = 2 value comes from solving a one-dimensional dynamical problem explicitly (the simplex is an interval), and for m >= 3 the extremal operator realising the threshold is not known even conjecturally; the threshold is an infimum over a semialgebraic set of operators, so exact values will be algebraic numbers of growing degree and there is no reason for a closed form.
attempt.key_identity: At m = 2 the general bound 1/(2m) = 0.25 exceeds the exact lambda_2 = (3 - sqrt(7))/2 = 0.177 by about 41 per cent, which calibrates the expected size of lambda_m as roughly (3 - sqrt(7))/m rather than 1/(2m).

title: Trajectories of quadratic bistochastic operators
statement: A quadratic operator V on S^{m-1} is bistochastic if V(x) is majorised by x for every x, i.e. the partial sums of the decreasing rearrangement of V(x) are dominated by those of x. Investigate the behaviour of the trajectories of the bistochastic quadratic operators.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on quadratic bistochastic (doubly stochastic) operators and their trajectories. The classification results of Ganikhodzhaev and coauthors on extreme points of the set of quadratic bistochastic operators are the main literature; a general description of trajectory behaviour was not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use majorisation directly: bistochasticity says V(x) is majorised by x, so every Schur-concave function increases along trajectories.
attempt.result: That gives the dynamics a Lyapunov function for free, and a canonical one: the Shannon entropy H(x) = -sum_i x_i log x_i is Schur-concave, so H(V(x)) >= H(x) for every bistochastic V and every x. Hence H is nondecreasing along every trajectory and bounded above by log m, so H(x(n)) converges; the omega-limit set of any trajectory is therefore contained in a level set of H, and any limit point y satisfies H(V(y)) = H(y), i.e. lies in the set where the entropy is exactly preserved. That is a genuine structural answer to the source's question, and it is elementary: the trajectories of a quadratic bistochastic operator are entropy-monotone and accumulate on the entropy-preserving set. In particular, if the only entropy-preserving points are the permutations of a fixed vector, every trajectory converges to that orbit. What this does not do: identify the entropy-preserving set for a given V, which is where the real classification work is.
attempt.obstruction: The entropy-preserving set can be large. For the identity-like extreme points of the bistochastic set, every point preserves entropy and nothing is learned; conversely for operators with a strict majorisation the set is the centre of the simplex. Deciding which case a given P is in requires the classification of extreme quadratic bistochastic operators, which is known only for small m.
attempt.key_identity: Bistochasticity means V(x) is majorised by x, so every Schur-concave function - in particular the Shannon entropy - is nondecreasing along trajectories, and the omega-limit set lies in the entropy-preserving set.

title: Historic behaviour of quadratic stochastic operators on a set of positive measure
statement: A trajectory has historic behaviour if the Cesaro averages of its iterates fail to converge. Find a class of QSOs for which the set of initial states giving rise to trajectories with historic behaviour has positive Lebesgue measure. The source notes that a similar problem was discussed by Ruelle.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on historic behaviour (Ruelle-Takens historic behaviour, Takens's last problem) for quadratic stochastic operators. The general dynamical-systems literature has positive-measure historic behaviour examples (Kiriki-Soma and successors) but I found none for QSOs. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the m = 3 counterexample of Zakharevich as a seed and ask whether its historic set has positive measure.
attempt.result: In Zakharevich's example (a = b = c = 1, the fully cyclic Volterra operator on S^2) the interior fixed point is a repeller and every interior trajectory spirals out to the boundary heteroclinic cycle, so the Cesaro averages oscillate for EVERY interior initial condition - the historic set is the whole interior, which has full measure in the simplex. So a class with the required property already exists in the source's own text, and the question's content must be the case where the historic set is neither null nor everything, or where the operator is not Volterra. Recording that the fully cyclic Volterra operator answers the literal question is the honest reading; if the intended question is a nondegenerate one (historic behaviour coexisting with a positive-measure set of convergent trajectories) then the target is a QSO with two attractors, one a heteroclinic cycle and one a fixed point.
attempt.obstruction: Producing coexistence requires an operator whose simplex splits into two basins, one of which is a stable heteroclinic cycle. For Volterra operators the boundary cycle is either attracting for all interior points or repelling, by the sign structure of A, so coexistence needs a non-Volterra operator, where no Lyapunov theory is available at all.
attempt.key_identity: For the fully cyclic Volterra QSO on S^2 the interior fixed point is a repeller and every interior trajectory approaches the boundary heteroclinic cycle, so the historic set is the entire interior and has full measure.

title: Quadratic stochastic operators that are eventually idempotent
statement: Bernstein's problem asks for a description of all QSOs with V^2 = V (Bernstein mappings, the stationarity principle or Hardy-Weinberg law); it was solved by Bernstein for m = 3 and by Lyubich for all m under a regularity assumption. Describe all QSOs which satisfy V^r(x) = V(x) for every x in S^{m-1} and some r >= 2.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the Bernstein problem for quadratic stochastic operators and on periodic Bernstein-type operators. The Lyubich theory of Bernstein algebras is the standing framework; I found no classification of the V^r = V case. Kept open.

attempt.method: Translate V^r = V into a statement about the image and the dynamics on it, before any algebra.
attempt.result: V^r = V says that V restricted to its own image W = V(S^{m-1}) satisfies V^{r-1} = id on W, so V|_W is a bijection of finite order r-1. Hence the classification splits into two independent parts: (i) the structure of the image W and the retraction of the simplex onto it, and (ii) the finite-order group generated by V|_W, which is a cyclic group of order dividing r-1 acting on W. The Bernstein case r = 2 is exactly the case where that group is trivial, which is why it is a pure algebra problem (idempotents of the Bernstein algebra). For r >= 3 the new content is a finite cyclic symmetry of W realised by a quadratic map, and since W is a compact convex-image subset of the simplex and V|_W is a homeomorphism of finite order, Brouwer gives a fixed point of V|_W and the action linearises near it up to conjugacy. That decomposition - retraction plus finite cyclic action - is the shape of the answer and is not stated in the source.
attempt.obstruction: A quadratic map cannot have finite order on a set with nonempty interior unless it is affine there, because the degree of V^{r-1} is 2^{r-1} and equals 1 only if cancellation is total; so either W has empty interior in the simplex, or V is affine on W. Deciding which of these occurs for a given P is the classification, and it requires the elimination theory that made the Bernstein problem hard already at r = 2.
attempt.key_identity: V^r = V means V restricted to its image W is a bijection of order dividing r-1; since a genuinely quadratic map has degree 2^{r-1} on iterates, finite order forces W to be degenerate or V to be affine on W.

title: Bi-harmonic functions on measured groups
statement: Does every measured group (G, mu) admit a non-trivial bi-mu-harmonic function, i.e. a function that is both left and right mu-harmonic?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on bi-harmonic functions for random walks on groups and on the Poisson boundary of a measured group. Found the standard Furstenberg-Kaimanovich theory and later work on the Poisson boundary; no resolution of the bi-harmonic existence question was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare the two one-sided problems, since a bi-harmonic function must be harmonic for both the left and the right walk.
attempt.result: A left mu-harmonic function is a limit of boundary data on the Poisson boundary (B, nu) of (G, mu) and a right mu-harmonic function corresponds to the boundary of the reflected measure mu-check. A bi-harmonic function is therefore a function measurable with respect to both boundaries at once, i.e. a joint invariant, and the question becomes whether the two boundary sigma-algebras have a nontrivial common refinement realised inside the space of bounded functions on G. This makes the answer immediate in one important case: for a SYMMETRIC mu the two boundaries coincide, so every nonconstant bounded harmonic function is bi-harmonic, and the question is nontrivial only for non-symmetric mu, where the two boundaries can be genuinely different. Restricting to non-symmetric measures is the useful reduction and the source does not state it.
attempt.obstruction: For non-symmetric mu the left and right Poisson boundaries are different measure spaces with no canonical map between them, so a common nonconstant function need not exist; constructing one requires a coupling of the two boundaries, and the only natural candidate - the double boundary of the bilateral walk - carries no invariant function by the Kaimanovich double-boundary argument.
attempt.key_identity: For symmetric mu the left and right Poisson boundaries agree and every bounded harmonic function is bi-harmonic, so the question has content only for non-symmetric measures.

title: A quotient space with no nonconstant quasi-harmonic functions
statement: Construct a countable measured group (G, mu) and an infinite-index subgroup H < G such that the quotient space G/H does not admit any nonconstant left (quasi-)mu-harmonic functions whatsoever.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on harmonic functions on quotient spaces of measured groups and the Liouville property for coset spaces. The Kaimanovich-Vershik and Rosenblatt criteria for the Liouville property on groups are standard; the coset-space version with infinite index was not found resolved. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what the Liouville property means on a coset space and where the standard proofs of it use the group structure.
attempt.result: On a group, the Liouville property is equivalent to triviality of the Poisson boundary and is proved via the entropy criterion (the Avez entropy of mu vanishes) or via amenability plus a Folner argument. Both proofs use the transitive action of G on itself by translations. On G/H the walk is still G-equivariant, so the entropy criterion survives in the form: the boundary of the induced walk on G/H is trivial if the conditional entropy of the position given the coset vanishes. So a construction should aim at a pair (G, H) with H so large - though of infinite index - that the coset walk is recurrent or has zero conditional entropy. The natural candidate family is G a wreath product and H the subgroup of finitely supported configurations, where the coset space is the base group and the induced walk is the projection, which is a random walk on an amenable group with the Liouville property. That candidate makes 'infinite index' and 'Liouville quotient' compatible; whether it also kills QUASI-harmonic functions, which are weaker, is the residual point.
attempt.obstruction: Quasi-harmonic functions are only asymptotically harmonic, so triviality of the Poisson boundary does not exclude them; the source's question deliberately asks for the stronger conclusion. Excluding quasi-harmonic functions needs a statement about the tail rather than the invariant sigma-algebra, and tail-triviality of the coset walk does not follow from tail-triviality of the walk on G.
attempt.key_identity: The induced walk on G/H is still G-equivariant, so the entropy criterion applies with the conditional entropy given the coset; a wreath product with H the finitary base subgroup has infinite index and an amenable Liouville quotient walk.

title: Sublinear drift on quotient spaces under ergodicity on the Poisson boundary
statement: Let (G, mu) be a measured group and H < G a subgroup which acts ergodically on the Poisson boundary of (G, mu). If d is a left G-invariant metric on the quotient space G/H, is it true that (1/n) sum_{k <= n} integral over G of d(gH, H) d mu^{*k}(g) tends to 0?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on drift of random walks on coset spaces and ergodic subgroup actions on the Poisson boundary. No resolution found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Interpret the conclusion as sublinear drift and ask what ergodicity of H on the boundary buys.
attempt.result: The quantity is the Cesaro average of the expected distance from the origin coset, so the assertion is that the walk projected to G/H has zero SPEED in the Cesaro sense. Ergodicity of H on the boundary says that the boundary carries no nonconstant H-invariant function, which is exactly the statement that the projected walk has trivial Poisson boundary - and for a walk with trivial boundary the entropy vanishes, hence by the fundamental inequality (Guivarch) speed times the growth exponent is at most entropy, so the speed vanishes whenever the growth of (G/H, d) is exponential. That is a genuine derivation of the conjecture in the exponential-growth case, and it isolates the remaining case: metrics of subexponential growth on G/H, where the fundamental inequality gives nothing. The derivation uses the standard fundamental inequality for coset spaces, which I have not verified in the literature in that generality, so the claim is conditional on that transfer.
attempt.obstruction: The fundamental inequality is proved for random walks on groups, and its coset-space version requires an entropy for a non-transitive action; if the metric d has subexponential growth the inequality is vacuous even on groups, and the source's problem allows any invariant metric.
attempt.key_identity: Guivarch's fundamental inequality (speed times growth exponent at most entropy) turns triviality of the projected Poisson boundary into zero speed whenever the quotient has exponential growth, leaving only subexponential-growth metrics.

title: Vanishing drift for conjugation-invariant metrics on symmetric measured groups
statement: Let (G, mu) be a symmetric measured group and suppose there exists a bi-invariant (conjugation-invariant) and mu-integrable (semi-)metric d on G. Is the drift delta_d(mu) equal to 0? The source suggests as a first test case the commutator subgroup of the free group on two generators with the stable commutator length.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on drift of random walks with respect to conjugation-invariant metrics and stable commutator length. The stable commutator length literature (Calegari) and the bi-invariant metric literature (Burago-Ivanov-Polterovich) are the relevant background; no resolution of the drift question was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use symmetry of mu together with conjugation invariance of d, which are the only two hypotheses, and see what they force.
attempt.result: Conjugation invariance means d(g,h) depends only on the conjugacy class of g^{-1} h, so the function g -> d(e,g) is a class function; symmetry of mu means the walk is reversible. The drift is then the limit of (1/n) E[phi(X_n)] for a class function phi that is subadditive along the walk. Subadditivity plus symmetry gives one immediate consequence: the walk is reversible, so E[phi(X_n)] is nondecreasing and the limit exists, and it vanishes if and only if phi(X_n) = o(n) in expectation. The special structure available here is that a conjugation-invariant semi-metric is a quasi-morphism-type object - by Bavard duality, the stable commutator length is the supremum of homogeneous quasi-morphisms - and for a SYMMETRIC walk every homogeneous quasi-morphism has zero drift, because phi(X_n)/n converges to a translation number which must be symmetric under inversion and hence zero. That reduces the conjecture, in the stable-commutator-length case the source names, to interchanging the supremum over quasi-morphisms with the limit in n. That interchange is the whole difficulty and is not justified here.
attempt.obstruction: The supremum in Bavard duality is over an infinite-dimensional set of quasi-morphisms with unbounded defect, and the drift of the supremum can exceed the supremum of the drifts; controlling the interchange needs a uniform bound on the defects that is not available in the commutator subgroup of the free group.
attempt.key_identity: A conjugation-invariant semi-metric gives a class function, and for a symmetric walk each homogeneous quasi-morphism has zero drift by inversion symmetry; Bavard duality expresses stable commutator length as a supremum of such quasi-morphisms, so the conjecture is an interchange of supremum and limit.

title: Isometric extensions of the Poisson boundary and non-ergodic self-products
statement: Let (G, mu) be a symmetric measured group with Poisson boundary (B, m) and let (X, xi) be an ergodic (G, mu)-space admitting (B, m) as a factor. Assume that the product of (X, xi) with itself is not ergodic. Does this imply that there exists a factor (Y, eta) of (X, xi) which is a nontrivial isometric extension of (B, m)?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on relative Furstenberg-Zimmer structure theory for measured group actions over the Poisson boundary. The absolute Furstenberg-Zimmer theorem gives the isometric/weakly-mixing dichotomy for measure-preserving actions; the source's question is its relative form over a boundary, which is not measure preserving. No resolution found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Recognise the shape: non-ergodicity of the self-product is the classical signal of a nontrivial Kronecker factor, so the question asks for a relative Furstenberg-Zimmer dichotomy over the Poisson boundary.
attempt.result: In the measure-preserving setting the implication is a theorem: an ergodic system whose self-product is non-ergodic has a nontrivial Kronecker (isometric) factor, obtained from the eigenfunctions witnessing the non-ergodic invariant function. The obstruction to importing it is precisely that a (G, mu)-space over the Poisson boundary is NOT measure preserving - the boundary is only stationary - so the invariant function on X x X produced by non-ergodicity is stationary rather than invariant, and there is no spectral theorem for stationary actions to produce eigenfunctions from it. Naming that as the single missing ingredient (a spectral theory for stationary actions, which is what the Furstenberg-Glasner theory of stationary joinings supplies only partially) is the useful step.
attempt.obstruction: Stationary actions have no unitary representation of G on L^2 preserving the measure, so the eigenfunction argument has no starting point; the substitutes (Nevo-Zimmer structure theory) apply to higher-rank semisimple groups and not to a general measured group.
attempt.key_identity: In the measure-preserving case non-ergodicity of the self-product produces eigenfunctions and hence a Kronecker factor; over the Poisson boundary the action is stationary, not measure preserving, so the invariant function is only stationary and the spectral argument has no starting point.

title: Joint queue length generating function for a two-queue gated plus one-limited polling system
statement: Determine the joint queue-length probability generating function at polling instants in the two-queue polling system in which one queue receives gated service and the other one-limited service (the G/1-L case). The source records the functional equation the pair (F_1, F_2) satisfies and notes that substituting z_1 = 0 yields a derivative, while substituting z_1 = h_1(z_1,z_2) leads to iterates F_1(h_1(h_1(z_1,z_2),z_2),z_2) with no apparent closure.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the two-queue gated plus one-limited polling model and exact analysis of polling systems with mixed disciplines. Boon-Boxma-Winands remains the reference for the open status; the boundary-value-problem literature for two-queue polling models (Cohen-Boxma, Fayolle-Iasnogorodski) covers other discipline pairs. Kept open.

attempt.method: Classify the functional equation, since the analytic method that applies is determined by whether the underlying branching structure is a multitype branching process with immigration.
attempt.result: Gated service is of branching type (each customer present at the polling instant is replaced during the visit by the customers arriving during its service), while one-limited service is not: exactly one customer is served regardless of the queue length, so the offspring generating function is degenerate. The mixed system therefore falls outside Resing's branching-type framework, which is precisely why the standard product-form solution fails, and the iteration the source describes is the symptom. What the equation IS is a two-variable functional equation with a kernel that is linear in one variable and of branching type in the other - the same class as the Fayolle-Iasnogorodski random walk in the quarter plane with one reflecting and one branching boundary. That identification points to the boundary-value method as the right tool and predicts a solution expressible through a conformal gluing function rather than in closed form, which is consistent with the source's failed attempts at an explicit answer.
attempt.obstruction: The boundary value method needs the kernel to define a Riemann surface of genus zero or one; with a gated component the kernel is not polynomial of degree two in each variable (the branching component contributes a composition rather than a product), so the surface is not defined and the Tutte-invariant or Riemann-Hilbert machinery does not start.
attempt.key_identity: Gated service is of branching type and one-limited is not, so the mixed system leaves Resing's multitype branching framework; the resulting kernel is branching in one variable and linear in the other and is not a genus-zero algebraic curve.

title: Large switch-over time asymptotics for polling systems with renewal arrivals
locator: Open problem 2 and Conjecture 4.2, PDF pp. 4, 5 and 7
statement: Prove Conjecture 4.2: a cyclic polling system with general (renewal) arrival processes converges to a deterministic cyclic system when the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity. The corresponding result for Poisson arrivals is known and rests on the multitype branching interpretation and a relation between models with and without switch-over times; the source supports the general case by simulation.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on large switch-over time asymptotics in polling systems with general renewal arrivals. The Poisson case (Winands and coauthors) is the standing result; no proof for renewal arrivals was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what the limit statement is really saying, so as to identify the minimal probabilistic input.
attempt.result: As the deterministic switch-over time S grows, each cycle lasts at least the total switch-over time, so the number of arrivals per cycle at queue i is A_i(S(1+o(1))), and the assertion that the system becomes deterministic is exactly a law of large numbers for the renewal counting process over a long cycle, plus the statement that the fluctuations do not accumulate across cycles. The first part is free for ANY renewal process with finite mean - that is Blackwell's theorem, not a branching argument - so the Poisson-specific machinery is not needed for the leading order. What the branching argument supplies in the Poisson case, and what is genuinely missing in general, is the second part: uniform control of the correlation between successive cycle lengths, which for a renewal process involves the residual interarrival time carried across the polling instant. So the conjecture reduces to showing that the residual-life process at the polling epochs is tight uniformly in S, which is a statement about the renewal process alone and does not involve the polling discipline. That reduction is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: Tightness of the residual life uniformly in S fails for heavy-tailed interarrival distributions with infinite mean residual life, so the conjecture as stated needs a moment condition that the source does not impose; with a finite second moment the reduction should be completable, and the general renewal case may simply be false.
attempt.key_identity: For large deterministic switch-over time S the arrivals per cycle satisfy a law of large numbers by Blackwell's renewal theorem for any renewal input; the Poisson-specific input is only the independence of successive cycles, which for renewal arrivals is carried by the residual interarrival time at the polling epochs.

title: Classifying the polling disciplines that exhibit the deterministic large switch-over limit
locator: Open problem stated after Open problem 2 (dynamic visit orders), PDF p. 7
statement: The source records, from reference [14], that numerical testing shows the same large switch-over-time limit theorems carry over to systems with Poisson arrivals and DYNAMIC visit orders, in which there is no pre-determined order in which the queues are served. The problem is the classification of polling systems, in terms of service, visit and scheduling disciplines, which exhibit this behaviour.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on polling systems with dynamic visit orders and large switch-over asymptotics. Found the numerical study the source cites and later work on dynamic polling policies; no classification theorem was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what property of a discipline the limit theorem actually uses, given the reduction in E0075.
attempt.result: The reduction there shows the limit needs only (i) a law of large numbers for arrivals over a long cycle and (ii) asymptotic decoupling of successive cycles. Neither mentions the visit order, so a discipline should exhibit the behaviour whenever the SERVICE rule leaves a bounded amount of work carried across a polling instant relative to the switch-over time. That gives a candidate classification: the deterministic limit holds for every discipline in which the work left behind at a queue after its visit is o(S) in probability - which includes exhaustive and gated service (work left behind is zero or the arrivals during the visit) and excludes k-limited service with fixed k, where the work left behind grows linearly with the cycle length. This is a proposed criterion consistent with the known Poisson results and with the source's simulations; it is not proved, and in particular the k-limited exclusion should be checked against the numerics before it is believed.
attempt.obstruction: For dynamic visit orders the sequence of visited queues is itself random and depends on the state, so 'cycle' is not well defined and the decoupling in (ii) has to be proved for a Markov-modulated sequence of visits; the natural regeneration structure (returning to a fixed queue with an empty system) may have infinite expected length under a greedy dynamic policy.
attempt.key_identity: The large switch-over limit needs only a law of large numbers for arrivals over a long cycle plus asymptotic decoupling of cycles, so the natural classifying condition is that the work left behind at each visit is o(S) - satisfied by exhaustive and gated service and violated by k-limited service.

title: Is the squared coefficient of variation of a Markov modulated Poisson process at least one?
statement: For an irreducible Markov modulated Poisson process (MMPP), is the squared coefficient of variation c^2 of the stationary inter-event time at least 1? The source records that this is folklore, that they initially believed it easy to verify, and that to date there is no known proof for an arbitrary irreducible MMPP.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the squared coefficient of variation of MMPP inter-event times and on whether MMPPs are overdispersed. The property is widely asserted in the applied literature; the source (Asanjarani and Nazarathy, 2019) states that no proof is known for arbitrary irreducible MMPPs, and I found no later proof. Kept open.

attempt.method: Test the conjecture on the structure the source gives: c^2 = d_2 - 1 where d_2 = 1 + 2 pi D D_Q^# D 1 in their notation, so the claim is a sign statement about a deviation-matrix quadratic form.
attempt.result: The conjecture is equivalent to the nonnegativity of a quadratic form built from the deviation matrix D_Q^# = integral over u >= 0 of (e^{Qu} - 1 pi) du of the modulating chain. That form is not a Gram matrix in general - the deviation matrix of a non-reversible chain is not symmetric - which is exactly why the folklore proof does not exist. For a REVERSIBLE modulating chain the deviation matrix is self-adjoint in the stationary inner product with nonnegative spectrum on the orthogonal complement of the constants, so the quadratic form is nonnegative and c^2 >= 1 follows. That gives the conjecture for all reversible MMPPs, which includes every two-state MMPP (all two-state chains are reversible) - and the source's own non-monotone hazard-rate counterexample is a four-state chain with a cyclic Q, i.e. non-reversible. So the honest statement is: the conjecture holds for reversible modulating chains, and the open case is exactly the non-reversible one. This should be checked against the source's exact normalisation of D_Q^# before being quoted.
attempt.obstruction: For a non-reversible generator the deviation matrix has complex spectrum and its symmetric part need not be positive semidefinite, so the quadratic form can in principle be negative; whether the specific vectors appearing (the arrival-rate diagonal D applied to the stationary vector) can realise a negative value is the residual question, and it is a finite-dimensional but unbounded-dimension optimisation.
attempt.key_identity: c^2 >= 1 is equivalent to nonnegativity of pi D D_Q^# D 1, a quadratic form in the deviation matrix; for a reversible modulating chain that matrix is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite off the constants, so the conjecture holds there and only the non-reversible case is open.

title: Stochastic ordering between the stationary inter-event time of an MMPP and an exponential
statement: For an irreducible MMPP, is the stationary inter-event time T stochastically larger than (or ordered with respect to) the corresponding exponential variable with the same mean, in the sense the source denotes T*_1 stochastically dominates T_1?
status_search: Same search as E0077. Kept open.

attempt.method: Relate the two conjectures, since a stochastic ordering is stronger than a moment inequality and the source presents them together.
attempt.result: Conjecture 4.2 implies Conjecture 4.1 only if the ordering is in the convex order, not the usual stochastic order: usual stochastic dominance between two variables with the SAME mean forces them to be equal in law, so if the two variables in the source's statement have equal means the intended relation must be convex or dilation order, under which the variance inequality c^2 >= 1 is immediate. That is worth flagging as a reading issue in the source's statement rather than a mathematical obstacle. Under the convex-order reading, the natural proof route is a mixture representation: conditionally on the modulating chain's stationary sojourn structure the inter-event time is exponential with a state-dependent rate, and a MIXTURE of exponentials is always larger in the convex order than the exponential with the same mean - by Jensen applied to the convex function t -> E[exp(-lambda t)]. That argument works whenever the inter-event time is a genuine mixture of exponentials, which is the case when the modulating chain does not move during an inter-event interval; the general MMPP allows the chain to move, and that is exactly the gap.
attempt.obstruction: When the modulating chain jumps during an inter-event interval the law of T is a phase-type distribution rather than a mixture of exponentials, and phase-type laws are not automatically above the exponential in the convex order - the source's own four-state example with a non-monotone hazard rate shows the failure of the simplest sufficient condition (decreasing hazard rate).
attempt.key_identity: Usual stochastic dominance between two variables with the same mean forces equality in law, so the intended relation must be the convex order; a mixture of exponentials always dominates the matched exponential in convex order by Jensen, and the gap is exactly the chain's motion within an inter-event interval.
